title: Lesson 74: Monolith vs Microservices vs Platform: When Salesforce Is the Integration Hub
description: The two independent axes of integration shape (code-splitting vs topology), Salesforce's own monolith-to-services evolution, the system-of-record test for hub status, and the governor and reliability limits that are the real cost of centralizing in the platform.

questions.question: A team splits its application into many independently deployable services, but every service still connects directly to every partner system with no mediator. Per the lesson, what has the team actually decided?
options: It has chosen microservices on the code-splitting axis but has not chosen a hub on the topology axis, so the point-to-point wiring problem remains unsolved.
It has fully adopted a hub-and-spoke topology because the services are independently deployable.
It has eliminated the need for a system of record because each service owns its own data.
It has made Salesforce the integration hub by virtue of splitting the code into services.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates two independent axes: how many deployable units the code splits into (monolith vs microservices) and which systems connect directly vs through a mediating hub (topology). Splitting into services does not create a hub; the point-to-point wiring problem from Lesson 8 remains unless something mediates.

questions.question: A company's official customer master lives in an on-prem ERP, and Salesforce holds a synced copy for the sales team. A consultant proposes making Salesforce the integration hub. What does the lesson say is the honest first step?
options: Name Salesforce as the spoke it currently is, or design explicitly to move the system of record, because hub status follows from where the authoritative copy actually lives.
Centralize all traffic in Salesforce immediately, since a synced copy is close enough to the source of truth.
Split the ERP into microservices so that Salesforce can become the hub without moving any data.
Reject the proposal outright, because Salesforce can never be a hub when any other system exists.
questions.explanation: The lesson's system-of-record test says the hub is the owner of the authoritative entity. If the ERP holds the official customer master and Salesforce holds a copy, Salesforce is a spoke. A hub proposal must either move the system of record or be honest that it is converging at a copy that can drift.

questions.question: A hub fans a confirmed order out to the ERP and the billing platform, and the ERP's fulfillment endpoint answers in ten seconds. Per the lesson, what is the correct design response?
options: Keep the call synchronous on the rep's request path, because a ten-second callout is within the synchronous budget.
Move the fan-out onto a platform event and let a Queueable or Flow drive it with a timeout and retry policy matched to the ERP, returning the page immediately with a processing state.
Increase the per-transaction SOQL and DML limits so the synchronous callout has more headroom.
Route the call through a bespoke microservices layer so the platform's governor limits no longer apply.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a ten-second user-facing callout against the synchronous budget is the wrong shape. The fix is to move the fan-out onto a platform event and let an asynchronous consumer drive it with a timeout and retry policy, returning the page immediately with a processing state, per the reliability guidance on operation-appropriate timeouts.
